Pool
pool
n. (a standing body of water, natural or built; rendering Hebrew berekah, agam, Greek kolymbethra)
Old English pol. In a land where water was scarce and cities were besieged, a pool was engineering rather than landscape — Hezekiah cut a tunnel to make one, and Jerusalem's survival depended on it.

Biblical Definition

A pool in Scripture is usually a built reservoir, and two of them frame the Gospel of John's theology of grace. The first is Bethesda: “there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches” (John 5:2), where a multitude of impotent folk waited for a stirring of the water and a man had lain thirty-eight years without ever being first. The Lord Jesus heals him without the pool, without the stirring, and without his asking — a picture of sovereign mercy reaching the man who could never win the race. The second is Siloam, where a blind man is sent with clay on his eyes: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing” (John 9:7). John pauses to translate the name because it is the point: the pool is Sent, and the One who sent him is Himself the Sent of the Father. Isaiah uses the image for the reversal of the curse in the wilderness — “I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water” (Isaiah 41:18) — and the historical books record the pools of Samaria, Gibeon, and Hebron as the fixed landmarks of a dry country, places where armies met and kings were killed.

Webster 1828 Definition

A built reservoir in a dry land. At Bethesda a man who could never reach the water first is healed without it; at Siloam, the pool named Sent, a blind man washes and sees; Isaiah makes the wilderness a pool as the curse reverses.

expand to see more

POOL, n. [Sax. pol.] A small collection of water in a hollow place, supplied by a spring, and discharging its surplus water by an outlet.

2. A body of standing water, without an outlet.

3. In Scripture, a reservoir constructed for the supply of a city; as the pool of Siloam, the pool of Bethesda, the upper pool.

4. In some countries, a small pond or lake.

5. The stakes played for in certain games.

Key Scripture

John 5:2 — "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches."

John 9:7 — "And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing."

Isaiah 41:18 — "I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water."

Isaiah 22:9 — "Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool."

Modern Corruption

Bethesda is preached as a lesson in perseverance — try harder and get to the water first — which reverses a narrative whose whole force is that the man never got there and was healed anyway.

expand to see more

The motivational reading of John 5 is remarkably durable: the man had an excuse ready, he blamed others, he should have found a way, and the sermon lands on personal initiative. Read the sequence. The Lord Jesus sees him, knows he has been long in that case, asks whether he will be made whole, receives an answer that is indeed a complaint rather than a request, and heals him regardless. The man does not know who healed him and cannot say afterward (v. 13). There is no faith recorded before the healing and no request. It is one of the plainest instances of unsought, unmerited, effectual mercy in the Gospels, and it is a poor exchange to trade it for a lesson in self-improvement. The pool with its stirring is the system that always favours the strongest, and Christ bypasses it entirely.

Siloam is corrupted in a different way, by treating the washing as the operative cause — a sacramental efficacy in the water, or a work the man performed to earn his sight. John forestalls both by translating the name. The pool is Sent, and the Gospel has been calling Christ the Sent One since chapter 3. The clay was made before the man moved, the command came from Christ, and the obedience was the means and not the merit. That distinction — obedience as instrument, never as ground — is the same one the Reformed confessions draw about faith itself, and this narrative teaches it in the concrete.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew berekah (a built pool or reservoir) and agam (a marshy or standing pool); Greek kolymbethra (a place for swimming or bathing, from kolymbao, to dive).

expand to see more

Hebrew berekah (H1295) — a pool, reservoir; used of the pools of Samaria, Gibeon, Hebron, and Siloam.

Hebrew agam (H98) — a marsh, standing pool; used in Isaiah 41:18 of the wilderness turned to water.

Hebrew shiloach (H7975) — Siloam, from shalach, to send; the softly-flowing waters of Isaiah 8:6.

Greek kolymbethra (G2861) — a pool for bathing; the word for both Bethesda and Siloam in John.

Greek apostello (G649) — to send forth; the verb behind John's translation of Siloam as Sent.

Usage

"“Whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in” — the system that always favours the strongest, and which Christ bypasses."

"“The pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent)” — John translates the name because the name is the point."

"“I will make the wilderness a pool of water” — the reversal of the curse in the vocabulary of engineering."
